name: Karl Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what is your shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I load reels of tiny components into a pick-and-place machine, which places them on circuit boards at an electronics factory. I finished secondary school and am still junior, so I check feeder numbers with the line lead before pressing start. The first good board looks simple, but one misplaced resistor can spoil a whole batch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Mei works at a library; our two school-age children and mortgage use most of our ordinary wages. We have about four months saved and some similar plants nearby. I use AI every day to look up part faults, but I check the microscope and the machine before changing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the board line that the AI error lookup saves time, and the microscope still matters. The pick-and-place machine puts parts down faster than I ever could. A misplaced resistor still needs the microscope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our circuit-board orders are holding, and my typical operator pay plus my wife Mei’s library wage covers the mortgage. We have about four months saved and some other electronics factories nearby, though I am still junior at feeder setup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep loading the component reels and checking the first board after every changeover. I would use the same AI lookup I use daily, and add a new small amount from full pay packets to the children’s school account after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I already work beside a robot, and a plateau would give me time to get better at the feeder numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error do you catch under the microscope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A resistor can sit one space over when a reel is loaded into the wrong feeder. I stop the run and ask the line lead to confirm the position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the school account a new saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The four-month reserve is separate. I would add money from this month’s wages only after the mortgage and food are covered.

say: I would tell the **board line** that error lookups still need a microscope check.
I would keep using my **existing AI lookup** for feeder faults.
think: Steady **board orders** and two wages cover our mortgage.
Four months saved and **some nearby plants** offer a reasonable search window.
do: Load **component reels** and inspect the first board after changeovers.
Add **fresh wage money** to the children’s school account after bills.
feel: **Calm**, with time to improve my feeder setup skill.
S0.quote: A misplaced resistor still needs the microscope.
fieldNote: Karl’s daily **AI lookup** is already part of his work, so continuing it is not new learning.
The children’s account receives **new wage saving**, separate from the existing four-month reserve.

steps.text: Keep loading component reels and inspecting first boards
Add new wages to children’s school account after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the plant should use better planning if it helps get the right reels to the line. I would also tell managers to show the night crew what happens to paid inspection hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI ordering could save office time, but improved cameras may mean fewer juniors checking boards. I am still slow at reel setup; my own hours could shrink even while Mei’s library wage holds, and the mortgage needs both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid place to learn the new AI defect alert if a guarded trial proves it catches wrong components. I would compare its marks with fifty first boards, keep my current shifts, and apply to posted nearby machine jobs at bill-covering pay after two reduced rosters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, yet curious about the alert. The four-month cushion lets me check a real opening rather than jump at a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the alert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put fifty known first boards through the inspection camera and compare its marks with my microscope list. The line lead would sign off any change to release checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower-paid job to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Mei and I can still meet the mortgage and school costs; I would compare the actual posted wage first. A new title does not replace cash.

say: I would ask to see **inspection-hour plans** before faster camera checks change staffing.
I would test a **new defect alert** against measured boards on paid time.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink as cameras improve.
Mei’s **library wage** cannot carry the mortgage and two school-age children’s costs alone.
do: Learn the **new AI alert** only in an offered paid place after a proven guarded trial.
Compare **fifty first boards** with microscope checks.
Apply after **two reduced rosters** only to posted nearby bill-covering machine jobs.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours despite a useful alert.
S1.quote: A new title does not replace cash.
fieldNote: Karl distinguishes his daily lookup from **new paid alert practice** on known boards.
His application requires **two cut rosters** and an actual local posting whose wage supports the household.

steps.text: Learn new AI defect alert if offered paid practice after guarded trial
Apply after two reduced rosters to posted nearby bill-covering machine job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the board crew thinking AI could plan production in 2028 when I am forty five, then capable hands-on robots could load and inspect boards around 2031 when I am forty eight. We need fault records before deciding who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect junior loading hours to shrink sharply when capable robots handle reel changes. Four months saved and Mei’s wage help us search, but neither can replace my pay through the children’s school years; the mortgage keeps the risk close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the next staffing notice and keep paid board shifts as long as they remain safe. If hours fall, I would apply only for posted nearby electronics work with bill-covering pay and paid safe instruction; I would also accept paid weekend catering bookings from former chef colleagues, but only if real customers book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a route to test. I would not buy kitchen equipment just because a robot is three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why weekend catering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cooked before factory work and still know people who organise family parties. I would take only paid bookings I can manage around the children, not promise a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run a robot trial now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a paid supervised place on scrap boards, with the guard and stop tested first. I would operate controls only if the plant actually offers that place and qualified instruction.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from 2031 hands-on board robots.
I would request **fault records** before junior posts are cut.
think: I expect **loading hours** to shrink under capable robots.
Four months saved and **Mei’s wage** provide time, not a replacement career.
do: Keep **paid board shifts** while safe and ask for staffing notices.
Apply after **lost hours** only to posted nearby bill-covering electronics work with paid safe instruction.
Accept **paid catering bookings** only from actual customers.
feel: **Anxious** about junior wage loss, with options to examine.
S2.quote: I would not buy kitchen equipment just because a robot is three years away.
fieldNote: His adaptive response adds **conditional paid catering**, not an assumed business income.
He requests a **supervised robot trial**, while any job application keeps posting, pay and instruction conditions.

steps.text: Keep paid board shifts while safe
Apply after lost hours to posted nearby bill-covering electronics job with paid instruction
Accept weekend catering only when paying customers book

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am forty eight, and capable board-handling robots come around 2034 when I am fifty one. Five years might be enough to qualify for electronic testing while I still earn on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tester could have more lasting work than a reel loader, but only if a real vacancy pays enough. My secondary schooling and daily AI lookup do not make me qualified to sign off a circuit board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present line shift and apply for a fully funded electronics-test course if the college offers paid workshop days and a practical bench place. After qualifying, I would apply to a posted nearby test role only if the wage covers our bills and its electrical safety duties are written; if none appears, I would stay on paid line work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the course and job have to be real. I like learning. The family cannot pay a mortgage with a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical testing mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a powered board with a qualified tester beside me after the safe isolation check. A video of a meter would not make me ready to sign a result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the college has only unpaid places?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue the paid factory shift and ask about a funded place later. Mei’s wage and our reserve can bridge a gap, but not weeks of unpaid study on purpose.

say: I would use **five paid years** to seek a genuine testing qualification.
I would keep **2031 planning AI** separate from 2034 board-handling robots.
think: A **test role** helps only with a real adequate vacancy.
Daily **AI lookup** is not a circuit-board sign-off qualification.
do: Keep the **paid line shift** while training terms are checked.
Apply for **funded electronics-test training** only if the college offers paid workshop days and a practical bench place.
Apply after **qualifying** only to a posted nearby bill-covering role with written electrical safety duties.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the course and job are conditional.
S3.quote: The family cannot pay a mortgage with a certificate.
fieldNote: Karl separates existing **AI use** from a new test occupation requiring practical qualification.
Course participation needs an **offered funded paid place**; the later application needs an actual safe job at adequate wages.

steps.text: Keep paid board-line shift while checking course terms
Apply for funded paid-time electronics-test course only if practical bench place is offered
Apply after qualifying for posted nearby bill-covering test role with safety duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am fifty three, with capable hands-on board robots around 2039 when I am fifty six. Thirteen years gives me time to build skill, but not a promise that the plant needs loaders forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be older, yet I may still owe on the mortgage and need a wage at fifty six. A tester role or a few paid catering weekends could help, but neither exists just because I put them on a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the board shift, ask about a funded paid test course and add fresh pay to school savings after bills. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare actual rosters and posted tester jobs; after a sustained cut I would apply only where the wage and safe duties cover our needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with time to try practical routes. I would rather count paid work than sell my family an imagined second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you open a restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A restaurant is a large loan and long nights, and Mei and I left that life behind. I would take small paid catering bookings only if they fit family time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for testing training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not out of the mortgage reserve. I would need an offered funded place with paid bench hours and a real local posting at a wage we can use.

say: I would explain **2036 thinking AI** comes before 2039 board-handling robots.
I would argue for **paid practical training** while the plant still has work.
think: At **fifty six**, I may still need a mortgage-paying wage.
A **test job** or catering income needs actual paid openings or customers.
do: Keep the **board shift** now and save fresh wages for school costs.
Check **post-2036 rosters** and apply after sustained cuts only to posted bill-covering safe test roles.
feel: **Uneasy** about later wages, with time to test practical options.
S4.quote: I would rather count paid work than sell my family an imagined second income.
fieldNote: Karl keeps **current paid work** distinct from conditional employment and applications after 2036.
His alternatives require **funded paid training**, posted safe work at adequate wages or actual catering customers.

steps.text: Keep current board shift and save fresh wages after bills
Apply after sustained cuts to posted bill-covering safe local tester role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could take junior board-loading hours around 2031 while our mortgage and school costs remain. Funded paid practical test training and posted local safe jobs at adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to sign off the first board after a robot loads every reel. A circuit board can look perfect until the wrong component heats up.

headlineQuote: A circuit board can look perfect until the wrong component heats up.
portrait: **Karl**, 43, is a junior electronics line operator with secondary schooling and daily AI fault lookup.
His **typical pay**, library-working wife, two children, mortgage, four months saved and some nearby plants provide limited flexibility.
He is **adaptive**, yet insists on paid practical test training, safe duties and an actual posted vacancy before changing roles.
Fast robots threaten **loading hours**; longer notice allows a conditional move into testing and small paid catering bookings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut Karl’s junior board-loading hours around 2031 while the mortgage remains.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded paid test training** and posted local safe jobs at bill-covering wages would help.
